item.title: Iran launches missiles at U.S. base for first time since Trump paused strikes
item.description:
Iran launched multiple ballistic missiles toward a U.S. military base in Jordan on Tuesday in what U.S. Central Command described as an "attempted surprise attack."

  • All of the missiles were intercepted, CENTCOM said in a statement.

Why it matters: This marks Iran's first ballistic missile attack against a U.S. base in the region since President Trump paused strikes against Iran on Friday to give diplomacy another chance.

  • The attack threatens to unravel the fragile pause and could force Trump to decide whether to resume military action.

What they're saying: Trump told Axios on Monday that the U.S. was in "very deep talks" with Iran but warned that he would return to "very strong military action" if diplomacy failed.

  • "Not much time," Trump said when asked how long he was willing to give the negotiations. "Either it goes fast or not at all."

State of play: CENTCOM said forces from Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) launched the missiles at 5:45pm ET.

  • "U.S. forces remain vigilant and at a high state of readiness," the command said.

The latest: CENTCOM said Tuesday evening that U.S. and Saudi fighter aircraft struck multiple logistics and weapons sites in eastern Iraq in response to what it described as more than 30 IRGC-directed drone attacks over the previous 72 hours.

  • Saudi Arabia's Defense Ministry later confirmed it participated in the strikes, saying they were coordinated with CENTCOM.
  • CENTCOM said the attacks on U.S. forces were unsuccessful.
  • There were more than 600 attempted attacks on U.S. citizens and facilities in Iraq by Iran-aligned militias between February and April, according to CENTCOM.
  • "The IRGC and its terrorist proxies must cease these attacks to avoid further U.S. military response," CENTCOM added.

The big picture: Earlier this month, Iran targeted a U.S. airbase in Jordan, killing two U.S. service members in a missile and drone barrage, prompting Trump to intensify what became a 13-night campaign of strikes.

  • Tuesday's ballistic missile attack by Iran came hours after Trump met Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at the White House for talks focused heavily on Iran. The White House described the meeting as "positive and productive."

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details throughout.

item.title: Thune and Johnson both plan to attend Trump's Dallas convention
item.description:
House and Senate Republican leaders are heading to Dallas to embrace the president who has done the most to shape — and complicate — their political fortunes.

Why it matters: Majority Leader John Thune and Speaker Mike Johnson don't have much of a choice about attending September's midterm convention. President Trump doesn't tolerate high-profile dissent, and both leaders know their best chance of staying in power is by staying united.

  • But for Republicans in tight races, the two-day political extravaganza presents a difficult choice.
  • They can stand shoulder-to-shoulder with Trump, raise money from big-dollar donors and bask in the MAGA media glow.
  • Or they can stay home and create some separation from a president whose approval ratings are sinking.

Zoom in: Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) and former GOP Rep. Mike Rogers, who is running for U.S. Senate in Michigan, are both planning to attend, according to people familiar with the matter. So is Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, another GOP Senate candidate.

  • However, Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), the only Republican who represents a state that President Trump lost, is unlikely to make it and will be campaigning in her home state, according to a person familiar with the matter.
  • Spokespeople for Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio), Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa), Rep. Mike Collins (R-Ga.) and Michael Whatley, the GOP Senate nominee in North Carolina, declined to comment or didn't preview their boss' plans. Hinson and Collins are also seeking Senate seats.

In addition to Johnson, Majority Leader Scalise (R-La.) and Majority Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.) plan to attend.

  • National Republican Senatorial Committee Chair Tim Scott (R-S.C.) and National Republican Congressional Committee Chair Richard Hudson (R-N.C.) are both scheduled to be in Dallas.

Zoom out: The Sept. 9-10 convention is still six weeks out, and senators and representatives have never been confronted with a mid-September, mid-cycle political convention.

  • Party committees are starting to ask donors about attendance, but details — and programming — are sparse.
  • "The upcoming Midterm Convention is an opportunity for Republicans across the country to rally behind President Trump's America First agenda that's brought lower drug prices, lower taxes, and a secure border," RNC national press secretary Natalie Baldassarre said.

What they're saying: "I'm proud that Dallas will host the RNC Midterm Convention this September," said Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas).

  • "Texas is leading the nation in defending freedom and advancing conservative principles, and I look forward to welcoming Republicans from across America as we celebrate the landmark victories achieved this Congress and work together to elect Republicans up and down the ballot in November."

The intrigue: For all the sniping between Trump and Thune this week, the majority leader recognizes that he and Senate Republicans stand a better chance of victory by presenting a united front.

  • But he'll be in Dallas during a Senate recess that the president wants canceled until the SAVE Act is passed.

The bottom line: The convention is expected to be part pep rally, part "Friday Night Lights": Clear eyes, full hearts — and Republicans hope the last line writes itself.

item.title: 86 senators vote to move forward with Graham Russia sanctions bill
item.description:
In a massive show of bipartisanship, 86 senators voted to move forward with a Russia and Iran sanctions bill championed by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham.

Why it matters: The vote came hours after senators gathered to honor Graham's memory, and immediately following a closed-door meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.

  • The vote was 86-12. Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.) was the only Republican to vote against it.
  • It is a procedural vote, but leadership hopes that the strong bipartisan support will allow for an expedited path to final passage.

The details: The bill had been led by Graham and Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) and reached more than 60 cosponsors this month.

  • The legislation would impose 100% secondary tariffs on countries that continue buying Russian oil and gas.
  • The bill also targets Russia's "shadow fleet" — the network of aging tankers used to evade Western sanctions while exporting Russian oil.
  • It was also updated to renew sanctions on Iran set to expire after the end of the year.

Between the lines: The sanctions package has long had wide bipartisan support, but concerns from the White House held it up for months.

  • Graham had been the key negotiator with the White House, trying to adjust language to ensure President Trump's signature.
  • After the senator's unexpected death, Trump indicated they would work to get the package done.

Zoom in: Some Democrats were hesitant to vote for the package, concerned about Trump's use of tariffs.

  • Zelensky and Finnish President Alexander Stubb gave compelling arguments for the need for the sanctions and tariffs package, arguing that Russia is in a losing position, sources tell Axios.
  • Zelensky watched the vote from the Senate chamber.

item.title: What's in the GOP megabill Trump is rallying behind
item.description:
House Republicans are pressuring the Senate to advance their reconciliation package as President Trump pushes for quick action.

Why it matters: The roughly $95 billion package is House Republicans' latest effort to enact Trump's priorities without Democratic votes using the reconciliation process.

  • The framework already cleared some early hurdles, but House Republicans are pressing the Senate to move quickly to keep Trump's legislative agenda on track before the midterm elections.
  • The reconciliation plan would require a simple majority in the Senate and avoid the 60-vote filibuster.
  • "We are ready to work side-by-side with the Senate to get this done for the American People!" Trump wrote on Truth Social last week.

Here are key elements of the plan.

Iran war and military operations

The budget bill instructs the House Armed Services and House Intelligence committees to draft legislation that could increase the deficit by up to $73 billion combined.

  • The Armed Services Committee has a cap of $60 billion, while the Intelligence Committee has a cap of $13 billion.
  • This would mainly aid defense priorities, which experts say likely includes military operations tied to the Iran war — a conflict that has already cost more than $37.5 billion since it began in February.

State of play: Last week, the House again rebuked the Iran war by passing a resolution to curb Trump's military campaign.

  • The vote came after three U.S. troops were killed in the region earlier in July.
  • The resolution is largely symbolic and carries no force of law.

Farm aid

The resolution allows the House Agriculture Committee to draft legislation increasing the deficit by up to $12 billion — funding expected to help struggling farmers.

  • This is separate from the Farm, Food, and National Security Act of 2026 that passed the House earlier this year. That package is still awaiting passage in the Senate.

What they're saying: The American Farm Bureau Federation celebrated the decision.

  • "We applaud members of the House of Representatives for recognizing the economic toll facing farm country and advancing farm aid as part of their reconciliation package," AFBF said in a statement.

SAVE America Act

The bill calls for the House Administration Committee to make changes to law that will increase the deficit by a maximum of $10 billion.

  • Because the committee oversees federal election law, any legal changes are expected to go toward implementing aspects of the SAVE America Act — a major political priority of Trump.

The other side: Elements of the SAVE Act funding have drawn criticism from some conservatives, who posit that the cash won't be used as intended.

  • Rather than including the full SAVE Act, the package offers grants to states to adopt voter ID requirements.
  • "That's just free money for Florida," Rep. Randy Fine (R-Fla.) said of the grant program last week, Axios previously reported. Blue states "will never take the grant money. I'm not a big fan of carrots. I like sticks."

Senate and the reconciliation bill

What's next: Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) has shown some resistance to the reconciliation bill, but House Republicans are increasing pressure on the Senate to pass the package, Axios reports.

  • Thune said he plans to wait until government funding is resolved before tapping into the budget resolution.
  • The White House is expected to turn up the heat on Senate Republicans, too.

What we're watching: Trump has publicly urged the Senate to pass the bill.

  • On Monday, the president urged Thune to keep the Senate in town until the SAVE America Act passes, another sign he's pressing senators to move quickly.

Go deeper: Democrats hit the anti-incumbency trap

item.title: Scoop: Trump asks Supreme Court to overturn $83M judgment for E. Jean Carroll
item.description:
President Trump's lawyers are asking the U.S. Supreme Court to overturn the $83.3 million defamation judgment he was ordered to pay to E. Jean Carroll, Axios has learned.

  • The judgment stemmed from Trump's 2019 statements in which he denied Carroll's claim that he'd sexually assaulted her in the 1990s and attacked her credibility, accusing her of making up the allegation.

Driving the news: Trump's lawyers argue he's entitled to presidential immunity because he made the comments while he was serving as president in response to reporters' questions, which centered on his fitness for office.

State of play: Trump's lawyers unsuccessfully appealed the $83.3 million judgment to the federal appeals court in the 2nd Circuit.

  • Now, in their filing to the Supreme Court, the president's lawyers — Robert J. Giuffra and Michael C. Martinich-Sauter — argue that the appeals court never decided whether presidential immunity applied in the case, and that the appeal was rejected on procedural grounds.
  • They argue that if the ruling stands, it will constitutionally weaken future presidents by exposing them to liability for statements made while in office.

The backstory: Carroll, a New York writer, in 2019 accused Trump of sexually assaulting her in a Manhattan department store in the 1990s. Trump denied it, setting off years of litigation.

  • In May 2023, a jury found Trump liable for sexually abusing Carroll and for defaming her in statements he made in 2022, awarding her $5 million.
  • In January 2024, a different jury awarded Carroll $83.3 million for Trump's 2019 statements.

What to watch: The Supreme Court is dealing with Carroll-related litigation for the second time in two months.

  • In June, the court declined to hear Trump's appeal of the $5 million verdict.
  • Trump's team has asked the court to reconsider that judgment.

Axios has reached out to Carroll's legal team for comment.

item.title: How the Supreme Court deepened uncertainty over Temporary Protected Status
item.description:
Legal protections for hundreds of thousands of Haitians and Syrians in the U.S. have ended after the Supreme Court upheld the termination of their Temporary Protected Status, a ruling that could reshape the program's future.

The big picture: The justices limited courts' ability to review Homeland Security's TPS decisions — making challenges harder and leaving hundreds of thousands of people at risk of losing legal status, work authorization and protection from deportation.

  • Established in 1990, TPS protects nationals of designated countries fleeing extraordinary circumstances.
  • "The ripple effects of this are going to be really big" and "really impactful for not only the TPS holders themselves, but for everyone in their communities," says Esther Sung, the Justice Action Center's legal director.

State of play: The Trump administration has moved to end TPS for nationals of more than a dozen countries, complicating legal challenges after the high court's decision.

  • At the start of President Trump's term, per the American Immigration Council, around 1.3 million people had TPS. Since then, hundreds of thousands have lost TPS protections.

What they're saying: DHS pointed Axios to government webpages on TPS, said recipients without another lawful immigration status will be subject to deportation "once TPS ends," and urged them to use the administration's self-deportation app.

  • "If people want to come to our country to work, they need to do that by coming here the legal way," a DHS spokesperson said Tuesday, rejecting the argument that ending TPS would hurt industries including health care, construction, logistics and restaurants.
  • USCIS spokesperson Zach Kahler said DHS was "upholding the rule of law" and argued the Biden administration improperly used TPS to extend protections beyond the program's intended scope.

Yes, but: The revocations are "absolutely without precedent, by huge orders of magnitude of any sort of revocation of status in the modern immigration system," says FWD.us president Todd Schulte.

  • Advocates warn the terminations could deliver an economic blow. Roughly 80% of TPS holders participated in the labor market, per a 2025 Penn study.
  • "I think people are going to really want to know why it is that the person who was their kid's teacher, the person who was a parent in their kids' classroom, left or got taken — or the healthcare worker, or the construction worker, the accountant," Schulte says.

What we're watching: TPS designations for nationals of other countries are also moving toward possible expiration.

  • That includes protections for some 170,000 Salvadorans, valid through Sept. 9 but potentially ending after over two decades.
  • "I don't have high hopes for TPS for any of the designated countries under this administration," Sung says.

Zoom out: Litigation over TPS terminations in Burma, Ethiopia, South Sudan and Somalia is ongoing, with challengers regrouping following SCOTUS' decision.

  • Last week, U.S. District Judge Brian Murphy temporarily delayed the termination of protections for Ethiopians, a move DHS general counsel, James Percival, framed as "mutiny against the Supreme Court."
  • But American Immigration Council senior fellow Dara Lind tells Axios: "The TPS challenges that are still working their way through the courts, even potentially future TPS terminations ... are going to have to meet a standard that the previous lawsuits haven't."

Zoom in: "TPS recipients are survivors," says Chris Newman, legal director for the National Day Laborer Organizing Network. He says recipients are sharing information and support on WhatsApp, Signal, and in Facebook and Instagram groups.

  • The consequences of stripping their status will be "calamitous," he warns — but he predicts it will galvanize public support.
  • "What you're going to see now, I think, are tons of mixed-status families, children with citizenship, employers, principals, pastors, full-scale revolting against this move," Newman says.

What's next: Those losing legal status face a reshaped immigration system.

  • Sung tells Axios: "This is the story of the Trump administration in immigration: It's trying to close the doors, and then all the windows as well."

Go deeper: Axios Explains: The past and present of Temporary Protected Status

Editor's note: This story has been updated with comment from DHS and USCIS.

item.title: "It's a serious clusterf*ck": Behind-the-scenes fury and panic roil key House primary
item.description:
While Democrats across the country are pulling their hair out over Michigan's brutal Democratic Senate primary, a key House race in the state is also quietly giving party leaders heartburn.

Why it matters: Infighting between establishment Democrats could create an opening for a progressive who many Democratic strategists and lawmakers are skeptical can win the seat in November.

  • Moderate Democrats and party leaders' inability to coalesce behind a single candidate has become the source of considerable behind-the-scenes acrimony, Axios has learned.
  • "This has gotten really intense," said a senior House Democrat, who, like others quoted in this piece, spoke on the condition of anonymity to offer candid analysis on the race and the anger surrounding it.
  • "It's a serious clusterf*ck," a Michigan state legislator told Axios. "I am just sitting back eating popcorn because now it's so f*cked up it's just, 'Let's just enjoy this.'"

State of play: Three Democrats are running in the primary to take on Rep. Tom Barrett (R-Mich.) in Michigan's 7th district, which President Trump won by just over a single percentage point in 2024.

  • Bridget Brink: A career foreign service officer who resigned as ambassador to Ukraine last year over Trump administration policy, backed by the Democratic Women's Caucus.
  • William Lawrence: A co-founder of the progressive climate organization Sunrise Movement, endorsed by the Congressional Progressive Caucus and Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.).
  • Matt Maasdam: A retired Navy SEAL and military aide to former President Obama supported by Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.).

What we're hearing: Slotkin, who represented the seat before Barrett, has rankled some colleagues and fellow Michigan Democrats by boosting Maasdam in the final stretch of the campaign.

  • In addition to recruiting Maasdam and then endorsing him and cutting an ad on his behalf last week, Slotkin has lent her name to his fundraising texts and paid for internal polling on his behalf, according to emails and texts viewed by Axios and multiple sources familiar with the matter.
  • A senior House Democrat said the frustration over Slotkin's push for Maasdam ranked some leading Democratic Women's Caucus members, telling Axios: "The Women's [Caucus] went apesh*t. And I mean apesh*t."

What they're saying: Several Michigan Democrats fumed that Slotkin's support for Maasdam risks eating into the lead that Brink has held for much of the campaign and creating an even larger opening for Lawrence.

  • State Rep. Jennifer Conlin, who described Slotkin as a mentor, told Axios she "found it so perplexing" the senator endorsed Maasdam given that Brink shares her background as a woman in national security.
  • "It's just very strange to me that she would be endorsing Matt," Conlin said.
  • Another local elected official expressed confusion at Slotkin's support for Maasdam because, they told Axios, the senator has told local allies "very plainly" that any Democratic nominee in the district "has got to be a woman."

The other side: "Senator Slotkin is singularly focused on one thing: flipping her old seat from red back to blue. Her entire goal is to help win back the House and put a real check on President Trump," said Slotkin spokesperson Josh Stewart.

  • Stewart added: "Matt Maasdam is the best candidate to do that."
  • Dianne Byrum, a former minority leader of the Michigan House of Representatives, said in an interview that the criticism of Slotkin for not supporting a fellow woman is "more noise than anything else."
  • "What we should be focused on is bringing out of the primary the strongest candidate to run against Tom Barrett, and I happen to believe that is Matt Maasdam," Byrum told Axios.

Zoom out: Centrist Democrats agree that Lawrence should not be the nominee for a key swing seat, pointing to his left-wing positions and his comments in 2024 that Black Democratic leaders "defang the white left."

  • Rep. Hillary Scholten (D-Mich.) told Axios that Lawrence's past comments "speak to a broader lack of judgment, temperament, and leadership that would leave him ill-equipped to lead in Congress. In short, he can't win."
  • "We have a great chance to win the seat if we get the candidate that can win the seat. Will Lawrence is not that candidate," said Rep. Brad Schneider (D-Ill.), the chair of the center-left New Democrat Coalition.
  • Brink and Maasdam "both would be wonderful," he added. "I wish the two of them were not running against each other but running in two different districts."

Yes, but: "Every election cycle, we hear the same inauthentic talking points against candidates demanding real change for their communities," said progressive Rep. Delia Ramirez (D-Ill.).

  • She added: "Voters are tired of empty suits reciting talking points from DC consultants or of those beholden to special interests, defending the status quo rather than delivering for the district."
  • Lawrence argued in a statement to Axios that casting him purely in ideological terms ignores the broader appeal of his anti-data center focus.
  • "If you don't live in Mid-Michigan, you don't know how angry people are about AI data centers pushing their way into our communities," he said, adding that his message is "reaching voters across the political spectrum."

The intrigue: As if the campaigns and their outside backers wailing on each other relentlessly wasn't bad enough for Democrats, now Republicans may be getting in on the action.

  • Brink's campaign and Slotkin allege that Michigan Sunrise PAC — which started running ads against Maasdam over the weekend — is a Republican front group, noting their bank is mainly used by GOP campaigns.
  • Michigan Sunrise PAC and the Republican super PAC Congressional Leadership Fund did not respond to multiple requests for comment.
  • "If Democrats care about winning back the House, they should unify around Matt Maasdam with the same energy as the GOP is expending to see him lose," said Stewart.

The race was already awash in spending from outside groups supporting all three candidates, including a Congressional Black Caucus-aligned super PAC spending $1 million on ads attacking Lawrence.

  • The largest spender in the race has been VoteVets, a group that works to elect Democratic military veterans to office, which has spent $2 million in support of Maasdam, according to Federal Election Commission filings.

The bottom line: Regardless of who wins, this is a primary that Democrats will be happy to wash their hands of after Aug. 4.

  • Said the state legislator who spoke on the condition of anonymity: "I think everybody's sitting back and saying, 'This is a f*cking nightmare.'"

item.title: Trump, Netanyahu tout "productive" meeting after weeks of tensions
item.description:
President Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu met in the Oval Office Tuesday for a "productive" 90-minute session on the Iran war — free of any public sign of tensions that have marked their relationship over the past several weeks.

Why it matters: The meeting could have gone the other way, given Trump's frustration with the Israeli leader over the war, which he even alluded to publicly shortly before Netanyah arrived at the White House. The fact that both sides described it as positive is a win for Bibi.

Driving the news: An account provided by the Israeli government stressed that the two leaders are in close coordination on the war and that there is no daylight between them.

  • "There is no truth in the claim that Israel is pushing the U.S. in a certain direction on the Iran issue," Netanyahu's communication director, Tzipi Hotovely, told reporters. "The Prime Minister is not telling the U.S. President what to do and is not pushing him in any direction. Both sides want to prevent Iran from having nuclear weapons. There are many ways to achieve this goal."
  • Aside from Iran, Hotovely said Trump and Netanyahu discussed the possibility of Saudi Arabia normalizing relations with Israel, which Trump called for as part of a Saudi nuclear deal.
  • The U.S. sale of F-35s to Turkey, which Israel opposes, was not raised at the meeting. And Trump did not demand that Israel withdraw troops from areas they are occupying, Hotovely said.
  • White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt confirmed Israel's description of the meeting, calling it "good and productive."
  • Unlike most of their previous Oval Office meetings, this one was private and reporters were not invited in. Netanyahu's office provided photos afterward.

What they're saying: Netanyahu said on Instagram afterward that his conversation with Trump today was one of the best they've ever had.

  • "We have a mutual understanding that the goal is to prevent Iran from getting a nuclear weapon," he said.

Context: After locking arms on the launch of Operation Epic Fury in late February, tensions have grown between the two men as the war drags on far longer than Trump predicted.

  • In a Fox News interview shortly before their meeting, Trump scoffed at the idea that Netanyahu was exaggerating the threat of nuclear activity at Iran's Pickaxe Mountain.
  • "I don't need Bibi to tell me that. Bibi's telling me that because he wants me to stay involved," Trump said.
  • Several other times, Trump has used colorful language to demean Netanyahu and insist he controls the Israeli prime minister. In late May, as Axios first reported, he called Netanyahu "f---ing crazy" during a call about Israel's actions in Lebanon.

item.title: Scoop: Nvidia's Jensen Huang meets Lutnick amid China scrutiny
item.description:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang met Tuesday with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick as the Trump administration investigates potential violations involving Nvidia chip exports to China, according to a source familiar.

Why it matters: Huang is in Washington as the Trump administration finalizes a framework that would give the government early access to the most advanced AI models before their release.

  • Officials are also weighing their approach to open-source AI and China.

Driving the news: Huang is holding meetings across Washington this week, including with Sen. Mark Warner (D-Va.), the top Democrat on the Intelligence Committee, and other members of Congress from both sides of the aisle.

  • Huang's trip had been previously reported, but not his meeting with Lutnick.
  • An Nvidia spokesperson said that Huang is in D.C. "meet with leaders on both sides of the aisle to discuss NVIDIA's work to strengthen the country's supply chain by producing $500B in American technology over four years and American leadership in AI, including leading in open source."
  • It wasn't immediately clear what Lutnick and Huang discussed.

Context: A Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security spokesperson told Axios last week that it's investigating potential Nvidia Blackwell chip export violations.

  • Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent last week also floated regulatory action against Chinese labs: "When PRC firms conduct covert, industrial-scale distillation attacks that cross the line into IP theft, sanctions and Entity List designations will be on the table," Bessent said.

What we're watching: The administration is expected to unveil its AI framework by Aug. 1.

item.title: AI is only "part" of high U.S. productivity growth, says Stripe economist
item.description:
AI appears to improve workers' efficiency in a number of sectors. The U.S. has experienced a surge in economy-wide productivity in the last couple of years. But the former isn't necessarily driving the latter.

The big picture: Companies are achieving more output per person-hour of labor because they are making better use of existing capital, a provocative new analysis finds — not, at the moment at least, by making major use of AI.

  • AI advances may be generating substantial micro-level gains in some sectors, but so far are not the driver of one of the most important macro trends of the last couple of years, finds Ernie Tedeschi, chief economist at Stripe.

State of play: A surge in labor productivity — after a couple of decades of subpar improvement — has been one of the best pieces of news about the U.S. economy in the last few years.

  • Over the last year, output per hour worked is up 2.5%, compared with 1.6% annually over the last 20 years, Tedeschi wrote.
  • That may sound like a small gap, but if sustained over just a few years, that higher productivity would compound, making incomes and output per worker much higher.

Yes, but: Tedeschi noted that while labor productivity is up, total factor productivity — not just output per hour of work but output per hour of work and unit of capital — is little changed.

  • Looking across industries, he finds that while sectors with high AI adoption do have higher productivity growth, that trend predates the pandemic — before high-quality large language models were widely used.
  • Rather, he finds, the higher output is coming from higher usage of existing capital.

Zoom in: "Think longer runs of factories already built, more utilization of server racks and GPU clusters already paid for, and more occupancy of existing hotel rooms," Tedeschi wrote.

  • "Economists call this 'capital intensity' or 'utilization.' Higher capital utilization represents real economic gains, but it's not the same as microproductivity."

Of note: None of that precludes the possibility that AI advances will generate major productivity gains in the not-too-distant future, as companies work through the workflow and choke points that have restrained their potential.

The bottom line: "It looks likelier and likelier that the U.S. is in a period of high productivity growth, and that AI is part of the story," Tedeschi tells Axios.

  • "But we need to be sober about how it's playing a role, because that will help us discern whether AI is just a temporary blip on the growth path or something more persistent and transformational."

Yes, but: Tedeschi noted that while labor productivity is up, total factor productivity — not just output per hour of work but output per hour of work and unit of capital — is little changed.

  • Looking across industries, he finds that while sectors with high AI adoption do have higher productivity growth, that trend predates the pandemic — before high-quality large language models were widely used.
  • Rather, he finds, the higher output is coming from higher usage of existing capital.

Zoom in: "Think longer runs of factories already built, more utilization of server racks and GPU clusters already paid for, and more occupancy of existing hotel rooms," Tedeschi wrote.

  • "Economists call this 'capital intensity' or 'utilization.' Higher capital utilization represents real economic gains, but it's not the same as microproductivity."

Of note: None of that precludes the possibility that AI advances will generate major productivity gains in the not-too-distant future, as companies work through the workflow and choke points that have restrained their potential.

The bottom line: "It looks likelier and likelier that the U.S. is in a period of high productivity growth, and that AI is part of the story," Tedeschi tells Axios.

  • "But we need to be sober about how it's playing a role, because that will help us discern whether AI is just a temporary blip on the growth path or something more persistent and transformational."

item.title: The U.S. is running low on blood. Here's why that's dangerous
item.description:
The U.S. blood supply has reached crisis levels, prompting the American Red Cross and the Surgeon General's Office to urge people to donate.

Why it matters: A prolonged blood shortage could delay surgeries, trauma care and other treatments that depend on timely blood transfusions.

  • The Red Cross says it has "less than a one-day national supply of type O positive blood," which is the most commonly transfused blood type. Due to the shortage, the organization is limiting distribution of type O blood to hospitals.

Driving the news: Blood donations fell to a four-year summer low in 2026, the Red Cross said on Monday.

  • Current supply is not keeping up with the demand for blood, which increases during the summer, the Red Cross says.
  • The Red Cross attributes the low turnout of donations to extreme heat, bad air quality and "widespread foodborne illnesses" hitting the country.

What they're saying: "Every donation has the potential to help save lives, and we urgently need everyone who is eligible to make an appointment to give blood as soon as possible," Chris Hrouda, president of Red Cross Biomedical Services, said in a press release.

Flashback: This is only the second national blood supply crisis, according to the Red Cross.

  • The last time was in January 2022 when COVID, winter storms and staffing challenges disrupted the nation's blood supply.
  • In 2024, the Red Cross said it faced an "emergency blood shortage," though stopped short of declaring it a "crisis."

How to donate blood

How it works: You can visit a nearby blood collection location to make an appointment. You can also contact the following:

  • Association for the Advancement of Blood and Biotherapies (website) — 301.907.6977
  • America's Blood Centers (website) — 202.393.5725
  • American Red Cross says eligible donors can book an appointment on their website. (RedCrossBlood.org) or call 1-800-RED-CROSS (1.800.733.2767).

Zoom in: Find a Red Cross or Versiti blood drive near you.

Perks and rewards for blood donation

The American Red Cross is offering incentives for donating.

  • Anyone who donates by July 31 receives a Fandango movie ticket, which will be worth up to $15.
  • The Red Cross is also offering a $20 Amazon gift card to anyone who donates in August.

Go deeper: A pro donor's guide to giving blood

item.title: Speak or resign: Beshear ups demand for McConnell health status
item.description:
Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear (D) demanded in a blunt letter sent to Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) and his staff that McConnell verbally address constituents and demonstrate his ability to serve or resign his seat.

The big picture: It's been more than 40 days since 84-year-old conservative stalwart McConnell was hospitalized and appeared outside photos released by his office. His lengthy absence and past health scares are fueling speculation about his capacity to serve.

Driving the news: Beshear wrote that he was also sending the letter to Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.), urging him to investigate McConnell's capacity to serve.

  • "I understand anyone's desire for privacy, but when you run for office and serve as one of a state's two U.S. senators, you willingly abdicate much of your personal privacy," the letter read. "That's the deal, and we all know it when we run."
  • Beshear concluded the letter: "All of this speculation and even this letter could have been avoided with a minimal amount of transparency," adding, "Kentuckians are just asking you to be honest."
  • Thune's and McConnell's offices did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment.

State of play: Under Kentucky law, Senate vacancies — which can occur due to resignation, expulsion or death — are filled by a special election.

  • McConnell will retire after his term ends in January 2027.

Catch up quick: The letter, dated Monday, is the second that Beshear has sent to the senator's office requesting updates on his health.

  • McConnell is still recovering from a fall at his home in June, according to a Monday statement from Congress' physician's office, which was released alongside a statement from the senator and a photo of him and his wife.
  • The physician said McConnell has undergone "strenuous" physical therapy and rehabilitation, adding that the senator's childhood bout with polio is a "significant factor in his mobility."

Friction point: Rumors and conspiracy theories have snowballed in the wake of McConnell's absence from public view, fueled by influential MAGA voices.

  • But McConnell said in the most recent statement issued by his office that he's "still working hard to get back to my full schedule of work in the Senate and in Kentucky."

Go deeper: Scoop: Democrat wants reckoning over McConnell, Kean absences

item.title: Six steps to socialism
item.description:
👉 Watch a video version of this column.

Republicans didn't decide to become President Trump's party. They surrendered to him, one stage at a time, over a decade, in plain sight.

  • Democrats swear that socialism's growing grip on their party is different, and can be contained. The early signals suggest otherwise.

Why it matters: Party transformations follow a predictable six-stage evolution — recoil, squint, rationalize, submit, amplify, and purge. Each stage has language you can hear long before you see it in the votes. Republicans just finished the full cycle. Democrats might be starting it.

Watch how the language shifts, stage by stage, for signs of whether recent socialist wins are an anomaly, or the start of something bigger and broader.

  • Stage 1: Recoil. Denounce, by name. Lindsey Graham called Trump a "kook" who was unfit for office. Ted Cruz called him a "pathological liar." That was 2016. Both later defended him against the exact words they coined.
  • Stage 2: Squint. Support without looking. "I haven't seen the tweet" became the go-to response of House and Senate Republicans in Trump's first term when they were asked about the latest storm. Some did the binary dodge: "The other side is worse."
  • Stage 3: Rationalize. This is the "yes, but" stage: "I don't love the style, but the judges ... the tax cuts ... the border ... He's a fighter." This is where accommodation becomes the norm, and the need to win trumps style or tactics.
  • Stage 4: Submit. Dissent becomes career-ending. House Republican Leader Kevin McCarthy said on the floor that Trump "bears responsibility" for Jan. 6. Two weeks later, McCarthy flew to Mar-a-Lago to make peace. In less than three years, he'd been ousted as speaker. Silence becomes life-and-death survival.
  • Stage 5: Amplify. Fully adopt the vocabulary, the style, the maximal claims. Try to out-Trump Trump. After privately calling Trump "America's Hitler" in 2016, JD Vance is now vice president. And routinely seeks to show his Trumpiness. That's almost every Republican now.
  • Stage 6: Purge. Actively work to oust anyone who disagrees. You either fully accept and amplify, or get exiled. Sen. Jeff Flake (R-Ariz.), Sen. Bob Corker (R-Tenn.), Rep. Liz Cheney (R-Wyo.) — gone. This year alone, Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.) was beaten in a Trump-backed primary, Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) chose retirement over humiliation, and Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) drew a primary challenger (and lost to him) after voting with Trump 99% of the time.

Zoom out and in: With socialism, the Democratic base moved first, as the base always does. Gallup found last year that Democrats viewed socialism more positively than capitalism by 24 points — the widest gap on record, and sharpest among younger voters.

  • All three candidates New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani endorsed won their June 23 House primaries, defeating two incumbents: Brad Lander over Rep. Dan Goldman, Claire Valdez over Brooklyn's borough president, and Darializa Avila Chevalier over Rep. Adriano Espaillat — the Congressional Hispanic Caucus chair, backed by House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries.
  • Sit with that: A Jeffries-endorsed incumbent lost to a democratic socialist. That's Stage 4 machinery switching on, with the primary electorate punishing the establishment side of the fight.
  • It's not just New York. In Colorado, 29-year-old democratic socialist Melat Kiros toppled 15-term Rep. Diana DeGette, who leans progressive.

Now listen to the language: "It's not socialism, it's affordability" is the left's "It's not the tweets, it's the judges." Textbook early sign of Stage 3.

  • Bill Daley — former Commerce Secretary and White House chief of staff — told us Democrats can't rationalize a candidate saying: "Oh, I didn't mean it when I said or agreed with a crazy idea a while ago." Instead, Daley said, they need to aggressively denounce "out-of-mainstream ideas and plans," and go after actual socialists by "shoving that platform up their noses."
  • In an op-ed for The Wall Street Journal warning Dems of the "Tea-Party Trap" that befell the GOP, Daley wrote: "Democrats are fooling themselves if they think a similar hijacking can't happen to their party."

The counterpoint: Socialism is widely seen by most elected Democrats as political poison. So this moment could prove fleeting. Four reasons for this:

  1. Socialism has no enforcer yet. Trump ended careers personally. An idea can't, unless someone becomes the idea. Mamdani endorsing, campaigning and toppling incumbents is what an enforcer looks like in beta. But it's hard to see Bernie Sanders or AOC taking this national.
  2. The far left has no Fox News synchronizing base and elites. In fact, it's safe to assume The New York Times, The Atlantic and MS NOW will resist socialism, at least initially. But watch for the formation of a media ecosystem to counter them. Politics is downstream from information flow and currents.
  3. Transmission is slower. Democratic voters, broadly speaking, are institutionalists. Republican voters wanted demolition. Submission to an insurgency may have a lower ceiling on the left.
  4. Socialists need to clear general-election hurdles, as Trump did. If socialist nominees cost Democrats swing seats in November, expect the Iraq-style reversal and recoil to come roaring back.

What to watch:

  1. The language: Do swing-district Democrats start saying "democratic socialist" without flinching or keep laundering it as "affordability"? Laundering means Stage 3.
  2. The endorsement lag: How long do Jeffries and Chuck Schumer stall on Mamdani-wing nominees this fall? Jeffries' slow-walk on Mamdani himself last year was textbook squint.
  3. The Liz Cheney test: Does a Democrat lose a primary specifically for attacking the socialist wing? That's the Stage 4 gateway.
  4. Copycat: Do 2028 hopefuls adopt the rent freezes and public groceries they mocked in 2019? Stage 5: Language + policies.
  5. Retirements: Do moderate Democrats retire rather than adapt?

That's Stage 6 starting.

📱 Share this video ... Subscribe to our YouTube channel.

  • 📈 If you're a CEO or on a CEO's team: Ask to join Jim's new weekly Axios C-Suite newsletter.

Go deeper ... Behind the Curtain: The cost of blind loyalty.

item.title: How Trump's "self-deportation" machine has ramped up
item.description:
President Trump's controversial "self-deportation" program, which pays unauthorized immigrants to leave the U.S., is on pace to account for more than 200,000 departures, according to internal data shared with Axios.

Why it matters: Launched last year alongside a multimillion-dollar ad campaign, the initiative is virtually the only carrot in an aggressive immigration crackdown that has been long on sticks.

  • Through July 16, the nearly $600 million program — dubbed Project Homecoming by the Department of Homeland Security — has helped about 132,000 people exit the U.S.
  • Roughly 70,000 more have signed up and are on track to leave, according to the data.
  • About half of the self-deportations have involved immigrants held in detention, under an effort that accelerated the departures and began when a DOGE staffer brought Project Homecoming into ICE facilities.

The big picture: The self-deportation program is a key part of the administration's push to remove 1 million unauthorized immigrants from the U.S. each year.

  • The idea was that unauthorized immigrants would be so fearful of being arrested and detained by ICE or Customs and Border Protection that they'd voluntarily leave the U.S., with the promise of free travel and a stipend of $1,000, paid once they had left.
  • The stipend has increased to $2,600 and was briefly $3,000 last Christmas.
  • Border czar Tom Homan said in May that encouraging self-deportations was "part of the plan from the very beginning."

Last year, then-acting ICE director Todd Lyons described the program as a way for the agency to "see our number" on deportations. But DHS hasn't released any official statistics to confirm its progress.

  • The government contract for the self-deportation program will run out of funds by the end of August, and DHS is seeking bids for another contract. The agency didn't respond to questions about whether there would any lapse in the program next month.

Zoom in: Project Homecoming started slowly, attracting about 24,000 immigrants in its first six months as staffers arranged deportees' travel documents and flights out of the U.S.

  • The White House then pressured DHS officials to move faster.
  • "The push was daily calls from the White House and weekly principal level calls [with Deputy White House Chief of Staff] Stephen Miller directly," one source said.
  • "They wanted like thousands pushed through on a daily basis, and we were putting through like dozens."

Behind the scenes: In August, a DOGE staffer aiming to shorten the time detained immigrants were locked up turned to the Project Homecoming team for help, and began taking its staff into ICE facilities, three sources with knowledge of the plan told Axios.

  • Case managers for the self-deportation program are now in 40 ICE detention sites, and about half of its 200,000-plus cases have involved immigrants in detention.
  • People in detention opting to leave the U.S. through the initiative now spend an average of 17 days in detention detained compared the typical 50 days, according to ICE data. That's begun to free up bed space in some detention centers.
  • "The administration for the first part of this thing had a bed-space shortage problem," said Todd Bensman, a former adviser to Homan. "You can't do mass deportation unless you have beds. They're inextricably tied."
  • "For the first time, someone walks in and goes, 'Hey, who here just wants to go home?' And everybody's like, 'I want to go home,'" one source said. "It's an immediate jump" in detainees seeking deportation.

By the numbers: Each self-deportation is costing the government about $2,500, plus the stipend paid to the deportee, DHS says. Removing an immigrant who doesn't volunteer for deportation costs about $18,245, the agency said.

What they're saying: "Thanks to the overwhelming success of Project Homecoming under President Trump, the CBP Home app has achieved far greater efficiency and participation than originally anticipated," a DHS spokesperson said, adding that DHS projects $2.5 billion in savings on removals costs thanks to the program.

  • A spokesperson for Salus, the contractor running the initiative, said the company "is proud of the humane and dignified support that it has provided ... We are committed to continuing to deliver for this valuable program."

The other side: Critics say the self-deportation effort would have been better run by the UN's International Organization for Migration, which promoted its work with the program last March but is no longer involved. IOM runs resettlement programs around the world and focuses on migrants' rights and international law.

  • "All of a sudden the whole program got reduced to a spreadsheet to buy plane tickets," said a source familiar with Project Homecoming who believes IOM would've done more to help deportees after they left the U.S.

  • "All of a sudden the whole program got reduced to a spreadsheet to buy plane tickets," said a source familiar with Project Homecoming who believes IOM would've done more to help deportees after they left the U.S.

item.title: UN's renewable-powered AI goal meets physical reality
item.description:
Data: International Energy Agency; Note: In terrawatt-hours; Chart: Amy Harder/Axios

A recent United Nations call to power data centers with renewable energy highlights a central tension in the AI boom: Renewables are rising, but so is reliance on fossil fuels.

Why it matters: Electricity demand for data centers is projected to at least double in the next four years, and where that power comes from will influence investments — and the trajectory of greenhouse gas emissions.

Driving the news: United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres is calling on all data centers to be powered by renewable energy by 2030, along with being more transparent on their energy, water and land impacts.

Reality check: Most energy analysts say the UN's goal would require rapid power-sector changes far beyond anything currently planned.

What they're saying: "There's no way to power every data center with renewable energy by 2030," said Michael Thomas, founder of Cleanview, a market intelligence platform. "That would require decarbonizing most power grids in the world in less than five years."

The other side: The goal "reflects both the urgency of the climate crisis and the speed at which electricity demand from AI and data centres is increasing," said United Nations spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric in an email.

  • "Renewables are among the quickest and most cost-effective options for expanding electricity supply in much of the world," Dujarric said.

Between the lines: Notably, Guterres framed the goal around renewable energy rather than carbon-free electricity, excluding nuclear power.

  • Dujarric said the initiative "is not intended to prescribe or exclude the broader energy choices available to governments."

State of play: Renewables are still poised to grow faster than any other power source. Power generation from renewable sources is set to surpass coal this year, the IEA said in a report last week.

  • Falling costs, rapid solar deployment and supportive policies are driving most new electricity generation globally,
  • This global trend is enduring despite President Trump's efforts to stymie wind and solar in the United States.

Zoom in: Renewable energy could account for more than one-third of data centers' total generation by 2030, IEA said in a separate report earlier this year.

Yes, but: The combination of two fossil fuels — natural gas and coal — still edged out the combined growth from renewable energy and nuclear power.

Zoom out: The UN's push comes as investors, policymakers and communities are pressing tech companies for a clearer accounting of AI's environmental footprint.

  • In recent weeks, Google, Microsoft and Amazon have all highlighted efficiency improvements in their annual sustainability reports, but the sheer growth is pushing overall resource use higher.

The intrigue: Thomas said tech companies could purchase credits of clean energy around the world to offset the emissions of their data centers powered by fossil fuels, "but it's important to note that this is largely an accounting exercise," he said.

  • Many hyperscalers are already doing this to some extent, but their emissions from data centers "are still rising because we live in a physical world," Thomas said.

The bottom line: The calls for transparency and data centers powered by renewable energy are linked, according to the UN.

  • "Ultimately, the initiative is calling on AI companies to demonstrate transparently and credibly how the expansion of AI can proceed without shifting carbon, water and land burdens onto communities and future generations," Dujarric said.

item.title: Anthropic, OpenAI blow past Starbucks, McDonald's amid AI boom
item.description:
Data: Company reports, Funda via "Key Context"; Chart: Ben Berkowitz/Axios

AI revenue is accelerating so fast that it's starting to dwarf some of the world's most recognizable brands.

Why it matters: AI infrastructure spending forecasts in the trillions of dollars start to make at least a little more sense when investors see how they're paying off.

By the numbers: OpenAI and Anthropic, combined, are on track for an annual revenue rate of about $120 billion, "Key Context" Substack author Tae Kim noted on Monday, via data from AI investment research platform Funda.

  • Anthropic makes up about 60% of that, given the company's lead with corporate customers (a lead that OpenAI is working to shrink).
  • Both would land in the Fortune 500's top 100 companies by revenue at those levels.

Stunning stat: At around $71 billion in estimated annual revenue, Anthropic would best Starbucks ($37.2 billion) and McDonald's ($26.9 billion) combined.

  • It would almost top both of them plus Taco Bell and KFC parent Yum Brands as well.
  • Those international brands are 50 to 100 years old, with tens of thousands of locations and nearly universal recognition; Anthropic was just founded five years ago.

The bottom line: Who needs to eat out when Claude can just give you the recipe.

item.title: A diminished Bibi arrives for his moment with Trump
item.description:
Benjamin Netanyahu will meet with Donald Trump in the Oval Office Tuesday for the eighth time since the president returned to office. But the Israeli prime minister arrives at the White House weaker and less influential than the previous seven times.

Why it matters: On Feb. 28, Trump and Netanyahu went to war together and it looked like there was no daylight between them. But exactly five months later, their interests have diverged more than ever — and bad blood and frustration have deepened as they've grown suspicious of each other's intentions.

Driving the news: Netanyahu's visit comes several days after Trump paused U.S. strikes in Iran and announced his envoys are trying — again — to negotiate a deal with the Iranian regime.

  • Last Friday, Netanyahu found himself holding marathon talks with his cabinet about the war — while largely in the dark about Trump's thinking and plans.
  • The lack of coordination led Netanyahu and the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) to prepare for the most extreme scenario: a return to major combat operations by the U.S. Only late Friday night did Israel learn that Trump had decided to hold fire.
  • Trump told Axios he is still considering resuming a large-scale military campaign if negotiations fail. Such a move would likely include a joint military campaign with Israel similar to Operation Epic Fury at the outset of the war.
  • The meeting with Netanyahu could be significant as Trump weighs his next steps, including possible coordination between the two countries.
  • But the Israeli prime minister is very aware of the narrative that he pulled Trump into the war. Even if it's too late to dispel it, he doesn't want to be seen as doing it again.

Behind the scenes: In the first few months of the war, Trump and Netanyahu spoke almost every day to coordinate and exchange views. But in recent weeks, their phone calls have become more and more infrequent.

  • Netanyahu started leaning more on Secretary of State Marco Rubio for updates on Trump's thinking, sources say.
  • Netanyahu even struggled to get on Trump's schedule for Tuesday's sit-down. He wanted to come to the White House last week but couldn't get an appointment.

Zoom in: Since the April 8 ceasefire, Netanyahu's influence over Trump's war policies and decision-making has been gradually diminishing.

  • Trump signed the memorandum of understanding with Iran in mid-June despite Netanyahu's skepticism. The Israeli prime minister tried but failed to convince Trump to keep fighting in order to further degrade the regime's military capabilities, U.S. and Israeli officials said.
  • When the agreement was signed, Netanyahu didn't come out against it publicly, hoping it would collapse on its own. It did several weeks later.
  • On Monday, Trump acknowledged some distance between Netanyahu and him on Iran. "We have a little difference, but pretty close," Trump told reporters on Air Force One when he was asked if he is on the same page with Netanyahu regarding the war.

Case in point: Two weeks ago, Netanyahu was unable to persuade Trump not to move forward with a deal to sell F-35s to Turkey.

  • "Nobody tells me what we should be selling or not," Trump said Monday, referring to Netanyahu's objections to the deal. "Turkey has been a tremendous ally for me. Turkey's not a big fan of Israel ... and not a big fan of Bibi."
  • Netanyahu was also caught off guard by the nuclear deal the Trump administration signed with Saudi Arabia last week. The Israeli prime minister was disappointed to learn that the language of the agreement didn't include a requirement that Saudi Arabia normalize relations with Israel — a provision the Israelis have long been pushing for, a Netanyahu adviser said.
  • Trump said last week the nuclear agreement would in fact be contingent on Saudi Arabia joining the Abraham Accords and signing a peace deal with Israel. But on Monday, the president acknowledged he hadn't talked about it with Saudi leaders.
  • The agreement is expected to be sent to Congress this week for review, but without any provision on Saudi-Israeli normalization, according to a source with direct knowledge.

Between the lines: Netanyahu is deeply unpopular in Washington these days, among Democrats, Trump's close circle and the MAGA base.

  • In public, Trump says his relationship with Netanyahu is still very good. In private, though, Trump has expressed frustration with the Israeli leader.
  • Many senior officials in Trump's inner circle have come to view Netanyahu with disdain, arguing he was consistently wrong about the war.
  • Numerous U.S. officials, including Vance, have accused Netanyahu of making rosy predictions that didn't pan out.
  • "He'll come, he'll make his promises and then we'll have to check everything out," a senior U.S. official said.

Yes, but: Netanyahu has managed several times before to go into meetings with Trump concerned and come out having gotten what he wanted, with Trump more aligned with him than before.

What to watch: Netanyahu is facing an election in three months that will be crucial not only for his political survival but also for his personal freedom.

  • He wants Trump to endorse him, but so far the president hasn't done it. Trump was asked by reporters four times in recent weeks whether he endorses Netanyahu, but he stopped short of doing so.
  • He praised Netanyahu for being a "great wartime prime minister," but each time referred to the Israeli prime minister in the past tense.
  • The meeting between Trump and Netanyahu is currently planned to be private and closed to the press. If he decides instead to go before the cameras, Netanyahu could leave with a triumphant photo op — or perhaps be on the receiving end of a Zelensky-style dressing down.

item.title: Canadians' travel pullback costs U.S. tourism billions
item.description:
Canadian travel to the U.S. fell 25% last year, according to a new Canadian government report, which says early 2026 data show the decline has persisted.

Why it matters: The report provides some of the clearest measures yet of the economic cost to the U.S. tourism industry after trade tensions, tariffs and President Trump's repeated "51st state" comments led many Canadians to vacation elsewhere.

  • "Following the change in the U.S. administration in early 2025 and the implementation of America First policies, Canadian travel sentiment shifted abruptly," the report says.
  • Statistics Canada says Canadians' return trips from the U.S. declined year over year for 11 consecutive months in 2025 — the longest sustained decline outside the pandemic since digital records began in 1972.

The big picture: Canada has traditionally been the largest source of international visitors to the U.S.

Zoom in: Canadians spent C$3.3 billion ($2.3 billion) less on trips to the U.S. in 2025, with lower leisure travel accounting for most of the decline, according to Statistics Canada.

  • Travel spending on visits to the U.S. fell to C$18.8 billion, down from C$22.1 billion in 2024, per the report.
  • Spending on overseas leisure trips, meanwhile, rose C$3.6 billion to C$22.8 billion, accounting for just under half of Canadians' total spending on trips abroad, the report says.
  • Representatives for the White House did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment.

Between the lines: Canadians largely redirected their travel rather than staying home, replacing many U.S. trips with domestic vacations or overseas travel, the report says.

  • The 7.1 million fewer trips to the U.S. in 2025 were offset by 5 million more domestic trips and 1.3 million additional overseas trips.

What we're watching: Statistics Canada data from April through June suggest the decline in Canadian travel to the U.S. may be easing after the sharp drop in 2025. The increase has been driven by automobile travel, while travel by air continues to lag.

The bottom line: Canada is only one piece of the U.S. tourism market. Upcoming U.S. visitor data should help show whether increased arrivals from elsewhere — including visitors drawn by the World Cup — offset some of the decline in Canadian visitors.

Go deeper: Trade fight splits Gordie Howe bridge celebrations

item.title: U.S. officials believe sanctions could hurt Iran more than bombs
item.description:
President Trump's economic assault on Iran has drawn a fraction of the attention devoted to his bombing campaign, even as senior U.S. officials believe it may ultimately do more damage to the regime in Tehran.

Why it matters: U.S. intelligence and open-source media reports point to a deepening economic crisis inside Iran, including gasoline shortages in one of the world's most oil-rich countries.

  • "The Iranians want to stop being bombed and they want money," a senior administration official said. "But that's almost in reverse order. They really want the money first."

Driving the news: Trump, who paused U.S. strikes against Iran over the weekend after 13 consecutive days of attacks, said Monday that Tehran had requested a meeting to discuss a deal.

  • Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei denied that claim.
  • Both sides are talking to mediators, led by Oman, Qatar and Pakistan, who are seeking to convert the pause in fighting into a durable new ceasefire.

Zoom in: A major focus of the talks is a proposal that would give Iran and Oman a measure of authority — and potential revenue — in managing traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.

  • The arrangement would draw elements from the cooperative framework used by Malaysia, Singapore and Indonesia in the Straits of Malacca and Singapore.
  • "Some of the Iranians want this. Others don't. That's part of the issue," the senior administration official said.

Iran wants assurances it won't be attacked again by the United States.

  • It also wants money — both unfrozen assets and freedom from U.S. sanctions and its blockade.
  • Trump is wary of rewarding Iran for disrupting traffic through the strait and is demanding that Tehran surrender its remaining nuclear material.

Zoom out: A second U.S. official acknowledged that sanctions and the U.S. naval blockade will take longer to force Tehran to the table than a full-scale bombing campaign, which Trump has so far declined to authorize.

  • That prolonged timeline could deepen Republicans' political exposure, leaving them to defend an unpopular war and elevated gas prices through the midterm campaign.
  • "I have a lot of patience," Trump told reporters Monday.

Between the lines: "Intelligence is picking up that the Iranians are complaining they can't pay their fighters," a U.S. official said. "Why? Because of the financial pressures. Because of Treasury. Because of what [Treasury Secretary] Scott Bessent is doing."

  • "They're in danger of runs on banks. There are gasoline shortages in this giant oil-rich country," the official added. "They're more scared of Treasury than the War Department."

Inside the room: In prior talks with U.S. negotiators Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, the Iranians made clear that gaining access to money was a central priority, according to U.S. officials.

  • "They're begging Steve and Jared for cash. They're desperate for it," one of the officials claimed.
  • The Trump administration has imposed sanctions on more than 1,000 people, vessels and aircraft under its revived maximum-pressure campaign, targeting Iran's oil trade, shadow banking system, weapons procurement and shipping networks.
  • Under its reimposed blockade, the U.S. is stopping, disabling and firing upon Iranian vessels.

The intrigue: Trump has said he paused the bombing to give diplomacy a chance. His decision also followed a warning from Joint Chiefs Chair Gen. Dan Caine about pressure on U.S. weapons stockpiles in Central Command, especially supplies of air-defense interceptors, sources told Axios.

  • The senior U.S. official described Caine's warning as standard military procedure.
  • "The overall stockpiles aren't depleted or at zero," the official said. "When you have to consider pulling from stockpiles around the world, that comes with risks, and you have to present that to the commander in chief. He decides. He's the decider."

Yes, but: Critics of Trump's war efforts say the president has few attractive options and question whether either military strikes or economic pressure will force Iran to accept his terms.

  • Iran generated an estimated $23 billion in oil revenue during the first half of the year — exceeding its budget projections — according to Brett Erickson, an analyst with Obsidian Risk Advisors.
  • "Economic warfare is a fundamentally broken approach to the Iran War," Erickson wrote Monday on X.

What they're saying: White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt told Axios that Trump "prefers a diplomatic solution, but he continues to retain all options if Iran continues terrorist activities in the Strait of Hormuz or against allies."

  • "Combined with successful sanctions that have crippled Iran's economy and 13 straight days of strikes against military targets in response to their repeated aggression, it would be wise for Iran to work toward a negotiated deal," she said. "Otherwise, they know what will happen."
  • Said another U.S. official: "The president has a win-win optionality. The U.S. is capable of prosecuting this militarily to the fullest extent. And the U.S. is capable to exerting economic sanctions that cripple Iran."

Go deeper: Trump to Axios: I'm ready for "strong military action" if Iran talks fail

The intrigue: Trump has said he paused the bombing to give diplomacy a chance. His decision also followed a warning from Joint Chiefs Chair Gen. Dan Caine about pressure on U.S. weapons stockpiles in Central Command, especially supplies of air-defense interceptors, sources told Axios.

  • The senior U.S. official described Caine's warning as standard military procedure.
  • "The overall stockpiles aren't depleted or at zero," the official said. "When you have to consider pulling from stockpiles around the world, that comes with risks, and you have to present that to the commander in chief. He decides. He's the decider."

Yes, but: Critics of Trump's war efforts say the president has few attractive options and question whether either military strikes or economic pressure will force Iran to accept his terms.

  • Iran generated an estimated $23 billion in oil revenue during the first half of the year — exceeding its budget projections — according to Brett Erickson, an analyst with Obsidian Risk Advisors.
  • "Economic warfare is a fundamentally broken approach to the Iran War," Erickson wrote Monday on X.

What they're saying: White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt told Axios that Trump "prefers a diplomatic solution, but he continues to retain all options if Iran continues terrorist activities in the Strait of Hormuz or against allies."

  • "Combined with successful sanctions that have crippled Iran's economy and 13 straight days of strikes against military targets in response to their repeated aggression, it would be wise for Iran to work toward a negotiated deal," she said. "Otherwise, they know what will happen."
  • Said another U.S. official: "The president has a win-win optionality. The U.S. is capable of prosecuting this militarily to the fullest extent. And the U.S. is capable to exerting economic sanctions that cripple Iran."

Go deeper: Trump to Axios: I'm ready for "strong military action" if Iran talks fail

item.title: Small businesses launch new Trump tariff challenge
item.description:
The small businesses behind high-profile legal challenges to President Trump's trade agenda are suing again to block his latest import taxes.

Why it matters: The lawsuits set up another legal test of Trump's tariff agenda after courts this year rejected one tariff regime and another remains tied up in court.

What's new: One lawsuit was filed on behalf of Burlap & Barrel, which previously challenged Trump's temporary Section 122 tariffs, and watch retailer Collective Horology.

  • The other was brought by toymaker Learning Resources, along with a flooring manufacturer and affiliated firms.
  • Learning Resources was a party to the consolidated Supreme Court litigation in which the justices invalidated Trump's emergency powers tariffs, though its own case was dismissed on jurisdictional grounds.

Catch up quick: The lawsuits challenge the administration's new tariffs imposed under Section 301 of the Trade Act, which took effect last week as the White House's temporary Section 122 levies expired.

  • The action generally imposes tariffs of 10% or 12.5% on imports from more than 60 economies that the Trump administration says failed to adequately block goods made with forced labor.

What they're saying: The Liberty Justice Center, representing Burlap & Barrel and Collective Horology, argues that the administration stretched what Congress intended as a targeted trade remedy into a sweeping global tariff regime.

  • U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer "determined the tariff rates first ... and assembled economy-specific findings afterward to justify them," the public interest law firm, which previously represented businesses challenging Trump's tariffs, alleges in a complaint.

The suit filed on behalf of Learning Resources says Trump officials relied on generalized findings rather than demonstrating how each country's practices burdened U.S. commerce, as the statute requires.

  • The complaint alleges that the administration imposed the same set of sweeping global tariffs after earlier legal defeats: "The third time's not the charm," the complaint says.

What they're saying: Collective Horology co-founder Asher Rapkin tells Axios that the earlier tariff regimes cost the watch retailer more than $160,000, with refunds from the earlier invalidated tariffs still outstanding.

  • "Section 301 tariffs are most definitely going to hamstring my business in the exact same way that the previous two phases of tariffs have," Rapkin says.
  • The company imports watches from Switzerland, where Rapkin says there is virtually no U.S. manufacturing alternative.

Flashback: Courts have already rejected Trump's first attempt to impose sweeping tariffs under emergency powers, while a separate challenge to his temporary replacement tariffs under Section 122 remains on appeal.

  • Now: The challenge has shifted from whether the administration has tariff authority to how officials are exercising their trade power.

The other side: The White House says the tariffs lawfully target foreign failures to block forced labor imports.

  • "Section 301 tariffs have proven to be a legally durable tool since the President's first term, and they remain so now," White House spokesman Kush Desai tells Axios in a statement.

The bottom line: Small businesses have been consequential players in the fight over Trump's tariff power, repeatedly forcing the administration back into court as it pivots from one legal authority to the next.

Editor's note: This story was updated with comment from the White House. This story was corrected to clarify Learning Resources' role in the Supreme Court litigation over President Trump's emergency powers tariffs.

item.title: Thune's shield against Trump
item.description:
Senate Majority Leader John Thune is pulling off something today's Republicans rarely attempt: telling President Trump "no."

Why it matters: Pressure from Trump and the MAGA base is piling up on Thune (R-S.D.), especially over a voter ID bill, but he has an important insurance policy: GOP senators have his back.

  • "I think he's got strong support. I read all the stories, but I think mostly that's made up by reporters," Sen. Mike Crapo (R-Idaho) told Axios.
  • "Leaders absorb some of the punishment, but I think he's doing great. No one could do a better job than he is right now," Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) told Axios.
  • "His cred in the conference has never been stronger," Sen. Kevin Cramer (R-N.D.) told Axios.

Catch up quick: Trump's frustration with Thune over the inability to pass the SAVE America Act or nuke the filibuster is, again, bubbling over.

  • "Thune should not allow the United States Senate to 'leave town' until it passes The Save America Act or, far better still, TERMINATES THE FILIBUSTER," Trump demanded on Truth Social on Monday morning.
  • Thune has snapped back, reiterating that it is a matter of math. There are not enough votes to pass SAVE, end the filibuster or justify canceling the August recess.
  • "Give me a rationale or a path to getting success, staying here through the month of August," Thune told reporters Monday about the calls from Trump and a few GOP senators to cancel recess to pass SAVE. "You could stay here til Christmas."

What to watch: Trump has not called for Thune's ouster. He even told reporters Monday that their relationship is "fine." But the building anger has fueled widespread speculation in D.C. that the president could eventually go there.

  • Even if he does, it would not carry the same weight as a threat to Speaker Mike Johnson's leadership in the House.
  • For one, Senate leadership elections are conducted by private ballot, giving more cover to senators who may not want to publicly cross Trump.

What we're hearing: Many Republican senators are quick to share their support for Thune behind closed doors, even if not all are willing to publicly do so right now.

  • Thune "is not in jeopardy," a GOP senator told Axios, requesting anonymity to speak candidly. "He is not the problem."

"We have a bunch of people across Capitol Hill that are obsessed with social media fame," another senator told Axios, referring to those questioning Thune's leadership.

  • Senior GOP aides for other senators also tell Axios the problem is really "squeaky wheels" getting more attention and that the situation could ultimately benefit Thune within the conference.

The other side: A conservative corner of the conference is certainly growing frustrated with Thune.

  • Seven senators are now calling to delay the August recess until SAVE is passed: Mike Lee (R-Utah), Rick Scott (R-Fla.), Ashley Moody (R-Fla), Jim Banks (R-Ind.), Tommy Tuberville (R-Ala.), Bill Hagerty (R-Tenn.) and Darline Graham (R-S.C.)
  • But even some of them admit Thune's leadership is not at stake.
  • "I wouldn't say that, because his job lies with us," Tuberville said when asked about any risk to Thune's position as leader. "But a lot of people are getting a little bit frustrated."

The bottom line: "I've been somewhat disappointed more Republican senators haven't been bold enough to speak out," Cramer said.

— Axios' Kate Santaliz contributed to this story.
